body.text: Unions have abandoned Labor during the Victorian election campaign
If Labor does somehow pull an electoral rabbit out of its hat at the Victorian election on November 28, it won't be thanks to the support of the state's trade unions.
In recent months, several unions have been either backing quietly away from supporting Labor, or just outright urging members to vote for someone else.

The retreat started late last month with the Electrical Trades Union (ETU) and the Australian Services Union (ASU) withdrawing support — the ASU even launched attack ads against Premier Ben Carroll, angry that he refused to remove a cap on council rate rises.
Other unions have followed.
Last week, Health Workers Union secretary Jake McGuinness reportedly told members he could not recommend a vote for Labor.
He also said he would meet with Jess Wilson to discuss workers' concerns, but had been snubbed by Mr Carroll.
Luke Hilakari from Victoria's Trades Hall Council accused Mr Carroll of "abandoned promises" as he gave the government a less-than-glowing review last week.

In a since-deleted Instagram post, the Victorian branch of the Maritime Union of Australia featured a member who said "workers are pissed off at the status quo, for sure" and urged voters to support a Greens or Victorian Socialists candidate.
Less surprisingly, given it has been in a bitter dispute with Labor for years, the United Firefighters Union urged Victorians to "put Labor last".
But political experts have also questioned whether losing the support of unions will ultimately make much of a difference at the ballot box, given the dire state of Labor in recent polls.

Senior lecturer in politics at La Trobe University, Nicholas Barry, said it was not necessarily unusual to see unions hesitant to publicly support an unpopular government — even if it was a Labor one.
"What's surprising on this occasion though is the number of unions that have basically been critical of the government," he said.
"Unions also play a major role in election campaigning, particularly by providing 'boots on the ground', that is, volunteers who can doorknock and hand out how-to-vote cards at polling booths.
"It is surprising that we've seen a number of unions reluctant to contribute in that way this time around and, in some cases, even running attack ads against the government as well."
In several cases, Victorian Labor's falling out with unions has come after protracted disputes.
Victorian teachers went on strike earlier this year for the first time in 13 years after a wage dispute with the government, while workers walked off the job at eight Melbourne councils in April.
Doctors and allied health professionals took industrial action last month, and the long-running and bitter dispute with firefighters shows little sign of being resolved.
The royal commission into construction sector corruption might be welcomed by most people in the community, but it is unlikely to win Labor many friends among CFMEU members.
"You've had three terms for all these resentments to build up. It does allow time for these grievances to build and that's what we're seeing now," Mr Barry said.
"The relationship between Labor and the union movement is historically very close but it's always fraught with tension as well and it's a difficult balancing act.

"Labor, in order to be electorally successful, needs to appeal to people who are a broader cross-section of the electorate on the one hand and is also constrained by economic constraints which hampers its ability to deliver all of what unions want."
Union support won't 'break the camel's back'

Whether the lack of support from unions will hurt Labor in the election is difficult to judge, especially as the party is already hurting from what polls suggest is a lack of support from the rest of the community as well.
Emeritus professor of politics at Monash University, Paul Strangio, doesn't think it will make much difference.

"The ties between the Labor party and unions aren't of the strength they once were and the trade union movement itself doesn't wield the same industrial or political muscle that it once did," he said.
He also argues "the tide is also running out" for Labor after 12 years in office.
"It's not really the straw that's going to break the camel's back for the Labor government, because of that political circumstance," he said.
"More broadly, I just don't think there's the same sort of traction out there in terms of trade union strength in the community that there once was."
He pointed to the industrial action by Melbourne tram workers in the lead-up to the 1992 election as an example of when unions held real power to sway the electorate.
On that occasion, tram workers blockaded the city for 33 days with 250 trams, backed by the trade union movement.
"That was a time when the unions helped bring the Labor government to its knees," Professor Strangio said.
"I don't really think that's comparable to the situation we're in today."
Who benefits from unions not backing Labor?
If it does make a difference somewhere, Mr Barry argues it could be in seats in Melbourne's industrial west and north.
"Those are ones that were hit particularly hard by the pandemic and the lockdowns and Labor's primary vote there collapsed, even though they won the seats," he said.
"They're the kind of electorates where One Nation is potentially a threat."
Several unions have already pushed members towards Greens or even Victorian Socialists candidates but Mr Barry said a drift towards the Liberals from unionists was unlikely.

"It's still a pretty major point of ideological division between the Labor party and the Liberal Party and the idea that the unions are going to find a Liberal government easier to negotiate with is highly unlikely," he said.

Negotiations with a Liberal government are something all unions are undoubtedly preparing for, and some may feel that process might be easier if it's not coming off the back of an election campaign where they've publicly supported Labor.
"When a government's about to fall, maybe you do want to put some distance between yourself and that government and the party," Professor Strangio said.
"They do need to be thinking forward and strategising and doing all those things in terms of what a change of government will mean for them, their relationship with the coalition.
"So all that sort of wargaming must be going on in trade union headquarters at the moment."

But that doesn't signal a longer-term shift away from unions supporting Labor, especially if — as Labor has warned during its campaign — a Liberal government embarks on cuts or wage freezes in the public sector.

"When Liberal governments are elected and if they bring in industrial relations reform, which happens quite often, what tends to happen is it can catalyse the union movement and unite them in opposition again," Nicholas Barry said.
Professor Strangio agrees.
A government hostile to unions may lead to a "feeling of besiegement of certain sections of the workforce", he said.
"It may drive trade union membership up, it may be a useful campaigning tool to enliven trade unions."
